plan: In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: you win whenever your value exceeds the second-highest bid (ensuring non-negative profit), and you never overpay since you only pay the second-highest bid, not your own bid. Bidding higher than value risks paying more than the item is worth if others bid between my value and my bid. Bidding lower risks losing profitable auctions. Therefore, I will bid exactly my value of $13.

This is a second-price auction with independent private values. The dominant strategy in a second-price auction is to bid your true value, since you pay the second-highest bid regardless of your own bid (as long as you win). Bidding exactly my value ensures I win whenever it's profitable (value > second-highest bid) and never overpay when I win. There's no incentive to shade my bid up or down. I'll bid my true value of $15.

This is a second-price auction (Vickrey auction), where the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own bid. In such auctions, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others' strategies. If I bid my true value of $47, I win whenever my value exceeds the others' bids, and I pay only the second-highest bid, ensuring non-negative profit whenever I win. Bidding higher risks negative profit if I win at a price above my value; bidding lower risks losing profitable auctions. Thus, bidding exactly $47 is optimal.
